extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy, psychology, and the scientific method (readers of Mill's System of Logic)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and methodological guidance for treating human thoughts, feelings, and actions as subjects of scientific inquiry; how to discover, justify, and apply laws of mind and the limits of such science. Emphasises inductive method, association laws, and the relation between psychology and physiology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science requires constant-law regularity
rubrics_metrics.description: Any facts are fitted to be a subject of science which follow one another according to constant laws, even if those laws are not yet discovered or are hard to apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use analogies like meteorology and tidology: absence of perfect predictability does not disqualify a domain from being a science. The essential criterion is lawful regularity, not current exactness of prediction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptability of non-exact (approximate) sciences
rubrics_metrics.description: A science may be inexact if the principal causes are known but many minor causes produce variations; such sciences can still yield general propositions true in the main.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine exact laws of major causes with empirical/approximate generalizations for minor causes, and allow for probable inaccuracy when applying predictions (examples: meteorology vs tidology).

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivation requirement for approximate generalizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Approximate generalizations in social inquiries must be connected deductively with the universal laws of human nature from which they result; they should be resolvable into properties of causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This connection shows the proper limits of approximate truths and allows deduction of new propositions for different circumstances rather than relying on blind empiricism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychology studies uniformities of succession among mental states
rubrics_metrics.description: The subject of Psychology is the uniformities of succession — the laws according to which one mental state (thought, emotion, volition, sensation) succeeds or is caused by another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These laws are discovered by direct observation and experiment upon mental phenomena themselves; classification of mental phenomena (thoughts, emotions, volitions, sensations) is foundational.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between laws of Mind and laws of Body
rubrics_metrics.description: All mental states are immediately caused either by other mental states (laws of Mind) or by bodily states (laws of Body); sensations have bodily antecedents but are themselves mental phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise both types of laws; do not conflate the phenomenon with its proximate physical cause. Sensations belong to psychology though their immediate antecedent is physiological.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological primacy of direct psychological study
rubrics_metrics.description: Mental laws must be ascertained by observing mental phenomena themselves rather than inferred solely from physiological data, since we do not yet know the characteristics of the nervous states that would ground such inferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physiology and psychology are related and both important, but discarding psychological analysis in favour of current physiological knowledge is an error; psychology can be more advanced in its domain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws of association (three primary laws)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas are excited by impressions or other ideas according to laws of association: (1) similar ideas tend to excite one another; (2) ideas frequently experienced together or in immediate succession tend to call each other up; (3) greater intensity can substitute for greater frequency in making ideas excitable by one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These elementary laws (Humean/J. Mill style) are empirical and form the basis for explaining many mental sequences and for constructing more complex psychological laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental chemistry / generation of complex ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: When many impressions or ideas operate together they may coalesce so that the resulting complex idea appears as one simple idea — a process analogous to chemical combination rather than mere composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between cases where complex phenomena can be resolved into elements by introspection (composition) and where they appear generated (chemical-like) and require specific analysis and experiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of Method of Difference to establish causation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Method of Agreement alone is insufficient to prove that a putative antecedent generates a mental phenomenon; the Method of Difference (experimental tests) is required to establish causation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For example, to show that certain associated ideas generate belief or moral reprobation, one must test whether introducing those ideas (difference) produces the effect; otherwise one only has correlational evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require direct experimental study of complex mental phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if complex mental phenomena are hypothesised to be generated from simpler ones, one must still study the sequences and properties of those complex phenomena experimentally and by direct consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: knowing oxygen and sulphur properties doesn't let you deduce sulphuric acid properties without experiment. Thus study beliefs, desires, volitions themselves, not only their putative components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of prediction: individuals versus masses
rubrics_metrics.description: Precise prediction of an individual’s thoughts, feelings, or actions is impossible in practice due to incomplete data and unique histories; but approximate generalizations about large classes or masses can be reliable and sufficient for social/political science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat general propositions as practically universal when they hold for the great majority; accept that useful social science rests on such approximations rather than exact individual determinism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate sources of individual differences carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: When confronting differing susceptibilities to psychological causes, examine whether differences are (a) original predispositions, (b) consequences of prior mental history, or (c) consequences of bodily (organic) structure, rather than assuming direct bodily causation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish effects mediated through different intensities of sensation (which then act by mental laws) from effects that would require positing direct influence of bodily differences on higher mental states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral freedom as self-formation feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: The consciousness of moral freedom consists in the feeling that one can modify one’s character if one wishes; a person feels free when they believe they could have resisted habits or temptations and could, by a sufficiently strong desire, change their character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To be fully conscious of freedom one must have some success in self-formation (confirmed virtue); the fatalist view is damaging mainly when it suppresses the desire to form character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habits and purposes as enduring causes of action
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions may become desired or willed independently of immediate pleasure or pain: a 'habit of willing' (purpose) can persist even when the action ceases to be pleasurable, and purposes must be counted among causes of volitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explains persistence of harmful habits after they cease to give pleasure and the perseverance of moral heroes who act despite suffering; consider purposes alongside likings and aversions when explaining actions.
